source.title: Noise-induced equalization in quantum learning models
source.authors: Francesco Scala; G. Guarnieri; Aurélien Lucchi

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some figure values are not stated numerically in the text.
record.tranche_reason: Extends the study of generalization effects to noisy quantum learning models and regression datasets. It does not test arbitrary-label memorization, natural-label classification, or the specific mechanisms named in V1–V8.
record.gate_note: The paper reports noise-dependent test MSE and training–test gaps for quantum regression models, and measures QFIM eigenvalue changes. These results concern a different model family and task from the claim versions. Cited results from other work were not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests quantum-noise regularization in quantum regression models, not any of V1–V8. It does not compare random and natural labels, sweep width beyond interpolation, compare architectures or optimizers, vary batch size, apply dropout, measure magnitude-aware sharpness, or remove memorized examples. QFIM conditioning is a different measure from V7's magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors report a correlation between QFIM noise-induced equalization and improved generalization, and propose a pretraining procedure whose estimated noise level is compatible with favorable test MSE in most tested cases. They acknowledge failures, including a substantial discrepancy for the overparameterized first architecture on diabetes. Strong noise suppresses sensitivity and can impede training.
record.recipe_differences: Quantum circuits trained on regression data with injected quantum channels; the paper studies quantum-noise regularization and QFIM equalization rather than the classical-network conditions and measures in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with noise channel and model regime; the diabetes overparameterized phase-damping result slightly mismatches the NIE estimate. The authors also report one discrepancy for the overparameterized first QNN on diabetes in the cross-validation analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: For sinusoidal quantum regression, NIE-based noise estimates generally lie near minima of test MSE across three noise channels and two circuit depths.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Moderate quantum noise can improve test MSE in the tested quantum regression models, with favorable noise levels associated with QFIM equalization.

fits_no_version.finding: For diabetes regression, NIE and test-MSE noise estimates generally agree, with a stated mismatch for the overparameterized phase-damping condition. This compares optimal-noise estimates rather than quantifying improvement over a noiseless baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining QFIM equalization can estimate favorable quantum-noise levels, with accuracy depending on architecture, dataset, and noise channel.

record.problems: The text notes finite test samples, finite training samples and parameter configurations, and a discrete set of tested noise levels. The generalization-bound Lipschitz estimate is described as quite loose. The main test-MSE results are plotted rather than numerically tabulated by noise level.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. QFIM eigenvalue-ratio measurements and training–test-gap comparisons were not extracted because they do not measure the specific outcomes named in V1–V8; the plots and tables also report noise-level estimates rather than per-condition generalization-gap values.

untested.parts: Coexistence of fixed-random-label memorization and natural-label generalization, including chance held-out accuracy under random labels.
Test-error changes when network width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classification, local connectivity, and convolution-derived initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance and dependence on tuning, weight decay, or optimizer switching.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce the large-batch penalty.
Dropout effects, small-data and excessive-dropout regimes, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its ranking of generalization gaps, and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus removing an equal number of random examples.

record.verdict_notes: States are assessed against V1–V8; cannot_determine does not deny the reported quantum-noise effects. Tables I–IV tabulate optimal noise levels, not test-MSE effect sizes. Agreement between noise-level estimators should not be treated as the magnitude of generalization improvement. No omitted result identified in the supplied text tests a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels for the specified image-classification models.
Width sweeps across the interpolation threshold for one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification models and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons on the stated image and language benchmarks.
Large- versus small-batch training under fixed epoch budgets and recipe changes.
Dropout effects and removing dropout and weight decay together in convolutional classifiers.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbation sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and comparing test accuracy with random-example removal.

rows.check: Test-MSE variation with quantum noise measures none of V1–V8. The reported dip does not establish an effect for a listed version.
